setup.zh: 开春，舅舅从县城来，念了一张告示：沉鼎观开山门，录为弟子者，家里每年五两银子。他刚念到「沉鼎」，你胸口的木牌烫得像一块炭。
setup.en: In spring Uncle comes from the county town and reads out a notice: Chending Temple opens its gate, and a disciple's family gets five taels a year. At the words "Chending" the token at your chest burns like a coal.

recap.zh: 舅舅带来了沉鼎观开山门的告示；他念到「沉鼎」，木牌烫得像炭——你决定去。
recap.en: Uncle brought the notice that Chending Temple would open its gate; at "Chending" the token burned like a coal — and you decided to go.

zh: 舅舅：簇新的青布长衫，二斤肉，一包红糖。
en: Uncle: a brand-new blue gown, two jin of meat, a packet of brown sugar.
"…present themselves for trial at the foot of Chending Mountain."
Between your fingers, a thread of silver light.

story.zh:
开春的时候，舅舅来了。

舅舅是你娘的亲弟弟，在县城济世堂做账房，是你们家这一门亲戚里，唯一一个"出息了"的人。他穿着一身簇新的青布长衫，手里提着二斤肉、一包红糖，站在你家漏雨的门口，拿袖子掩着鼻子咳了一声。

你爹慌慌张张地拿袖子擦了擦炕沿，请他坐。

舅舅坐下了，屁股只沾了半边。他看了看屋顶，看了看墙角接水的盆，又看了看你爹缠着麻布的膝盖，什么都没说，只是叹了口气。

吃饭的时候，他从怀里摸出一张折得方方正正的纸。

「县城贴的告示，」他说，「我抄了一份。」

他清了清嗓子，念：

「**沉鼎观，三年一开山门，收徒。凡十二至十六岁，身家清白者，皆可于九月初九，赴泗水沉鼎山下应试。录为弟子者，其家每岁由观中发给白银五两。**」

他刚念到"沉鼎"两个字——

你胸口的木牌，烫得像一块刚从灶膛里扒出来的炭。

你差点叫出声来。你死死按住胸口，低下头，假装被饭呛着了，咳个不停。

「这孩子，」舅舅皱着眉，「吃饭都吃不利索。」

没有人看见，你按在胸口的手指缝里，漏出一线银光。

那条银色的尾巴，不再是一明一暗了。它亮着，一直亮着，亮得发烫——像一个在梦里找了很久很久的人，终于听见了自己要找的名字。

「五两银子，」你娘轻声重复了一遍。

「五两，」舅舅说，「一年五两。」

你爹放下了筷子。你家一年交马家的租，折成银子，二两多一点。

「还有，」舅舅压低了声音，「家里有孩子进了仙门的，马家……不敢收租。」

屋里静了。

「姐，」舅舅转向你娘，「二十年前，我也去过。」

你们都愣住了。

「三百级石阶，」舅舅说，「我爬到一百六十级，腿就动不了了。我在那儿坐了一炷香，看着别人一个一个从我身边走过去。」他笑了一下，笑得很难看，「然后我就下山了，去济世堂学打算盘。」

他看着你。

「你娘识字，你随她，脑子比我活。你爹打猎，你随他，腿脚比我稳。」他说，「去试试。进不去，也不亏什么。进去了——」

他没说完。他看了一眼你爹的膝盖，看了一眼墙角的盆，又低头吃饭了。
story.en:
When spring comes, Uncle comes.

Uncle is your mother's own younger brother, bookkeeper at Jishi Hall in the county town — the only one in all your family's kin who has "made something of himself." He stands at your leaking door in a brand-new blue cotton gown, two jin of meat and a packet of brown sugar in his hands, and coughs once behind his sleeve.

Your father hurriedly wipes the edge of the brick bed with his sleeve and asks him to sit.

Uncle sits, perched on the very edge. He looks at the roof, at the basins in the corner that catch the leaks, at the hemp wound round your father's knee, says nothing, and only sighs.

At the meal he takes a neatly folded paper from inside his gown.

"A notice they put up in town," he says. "I copied it."

He clears his throat and reads:

"**Chending Temple opens its gate once in three years to take disciples. All between twelve and sixteen years of age, of clean family, may present themselves for trial at the foot of Chending Mountain on the Si, on the ninth day of the ninth month. The family of any taken as a disciple shall receive from the temple five taels of silver each year.**"

The instant he reads the word "Chending" —

the token at your chest burns like a coal just raked out of the stove.

You nearly cry out. You press your hand hard against your chest, duck your head and pretend you've choked on your rice, coughing and coughing.

"This child," says Uncle with a frown, "can't even eat a meal properly."

Nobody sees the thread of silver light leaking between the fingers pressed to your chest.

That silver tail is no longer bright-then-dim. It is lit, and stays lit, burning hot — like someone who has searched a very long time in a dream and at last hears the name they were looking for.

"Five taels of silver," your mother repeats, softly.

"Five," says Uncle. "Five taels a year."

Your father puts down his chopsticks. Your family's yearly rent to the Mas, reckoned in silver, is a little over two taels.

"And," Uncle lowers his voice, "a family with a child in an immortals' sect — the Mas wouldn't dare collect rent from them."

The room goes quiet.

"Sister," Uncle says, turning to your mother, "twenty years ago, I went too."

All of you stare at him.

"Three hundred steps," says Uncle. "I got to the hundred-and-sixtieth and my legs wouldn't move. I sat there for a stick of incense and watched the others go past me one by one." He smiles, and it's an ugly smile. "Then I came down the mountain and went to Jishi Hall to learn the abacus."

He looks at you.

"Your mother reads, and you take after her — you've a quicker head than me. Your father hunts, and you take after him — your legs are steadier than mine," he says. "Go and try. If you don't get in, you've lost nothing. If you do —"

He doesn't finish. He glances at your father's knee, at the basins in the corner, and bends over his rice again.

exits.means: decides to go to the temple trials

story.zh:
那天夜里，你躺在炕上，一直睁着眼睛。

你在心里算账——像你娘教你的那样，一笔一笔地算。

五两银子。一年。你爹再也不用拖着那条腿进深山。你娘下雨天再也不用把家里所有的盆摆出来。马三的短棍，再也敲不到你家的门框。

然后，是另一笔账。

木牌上那条尾巴，还亮着。它从来没有亮得这么久过。

你把木牌从衣领里掏出来，贴在耳朵边上，听。

什么都听不见。可你知道，它在等你。

「好，」你对着黑暗说，「我去。」
story.en:
That night you lie on the brick bed with your eyes open.

You do the accounts in your head — the way your mother taught you, one entry at a time.

Five taels of silver. A year. Your father never again dragging that leg into the deep mountains. Your mother never again setting out every basin in the house when it rains. Ma San's club never again rapping your door frame.

Then, the other account.

The tail on the token is still lit. It has never stayed lit so long.

You take the token out from your collar and hold it to your ear, and listen.

You hear nothing. But you know it is waiting for you.

"All right," you say to the dark. "I'll go."

exits.means: hesitates, decides not to go yet, waits

story.zh:
「不去，」你在心里说，「家里离不开我。再等三年。」

胸口的木牌，一下子凉了。

那条亮了一整晚的尾巴，暗下去，一明，一暗，一明——暗下去的那一下，比平时长。

你躺着，睁着眼睛，一直到天亮。你爹的咳嗽，隔着一道布帘，响了半夜。
story.en:
"No," you tell yourself. "They can't manage without me at home. Three more years."

The token at your chest goes cold at once.

The tail that has been lit all night dims — bright, dim, bright — and the dim lasts longer than it ever has.

You lie there with your eyes open until dawn. Through the cloth curtain, your father's cough goes on half the night.
